svg.text: Two cars with identical weight distribution, behaving differently
Both are 43% on the front axle. Both weigh the same. Both have the same tires and the same understeer gradient. The only difference is how far the mass sits from the middle of the car.
Same steering input at the same speed. The one with its mass gathered near the centre answers the wheel sooner and settles sooner.
low polar moment — a mid-engine car
high polar moment — engine over one axle, or hanging past it
Both cars have an understeer gradient of -0.24 deg/g — identical, because that is set by balance and these two have the same balance.
Steady-state behaviour is the same. Everything about how they GET there is different. That is the distinction this episode exists for.
What this does NOT show is twitchiness. Overshoot is 0.23% and 0.14% — the low-inertia car overshoots more, which is the textbook direction, but both numbers are so small that
neither car meaningfully overshoots at all. A 3 degree step at constant speed is a gentle input; "nervous at the limit" is a claim about large inputs and a driver in the loop, and this is neither.

[MEASURED] bicycle model (transient) + double-track (lap time) + Sedan_Pac02Tire.tir - m 1360 kg held fixed - [SOURCED] i_zz range 0.75-1.40x, RV-1 params §2 - layout archetype values [ASSUMED] §2 - drag off during the step, as in D4
Mass blobs are a schematic of distribution, not a mass model: polar moment goes as mass times distance squared, so the same total mass further out is a larger number. The yaw traces are measured.
